reviews.author: Youngki Cha
reviews.text:
I went to the Leeum Museum of Art during the Chuseok holiday. It is a place with such a reputation that many people visit it even during the holidays, and I can understand why.

Best viewing convenience & immersion
We recommend renting earphones when viewing the work. If you press the number next to the work, you can hear a detailed explanation, allowing you to enjoy the work comfortably and in depth as if you were walking with a docent. As I became aware of the historical background and meaning behind each piece, my level of immersion in the work increased significantly.

An encounter with the hottest masterpieces these days
The work that impressed me the most during this visit was by far the highlight of Joseon Dynasty painting. This work has become more famous thanks to a recent drama, and the humorous expression of the dynamic tiger and the magpie flying above it was excellent. The energy and detail felt in the painting was an emotion that could never be captured in a photo or video. (The majesty of K-art!)

From ancient art to contemporary art, perfect curation
Leeum has a really good balance of collections of ancient art (Museum 1) and modern art (Museum 2). The great attraction is that you can see masterpieces from various eras in one place, from the beauty of traditional crafts and paintings to experimental and sensuous modern installation art. Anyone who wants to understand the trends of contemporary art or feel the depth of Korean art history will be satisfied.

It was a valuable time where I was able to understand and appreciate the masterpieces without difficulty thanks to the well-equipped explanation (earphone guide). It was especially memorable because I was able to see Hojakdo Island in person, which goes well with the holiday atmosphere. Highly recommended for those who want to experience cultural richness in downtown Seoul!

reviews.author: World Travelist
reviews.text:
Lehman Muffin Seoul will be hosting Andy St. Louis's event from January 22nd to March 15th. In this exhibition, landscape painting is an inflection point that opens up a new style of perception. This exhibition, which brings together works by Kim Yun-sin, Kim Chang-eok, Hong Soon-myeong, and Scott Caan, focuses on the potential of landscape painting, that is, the transformed way images mediate the experience of the natural environment.

Kim Chang-eok (1920-1997) was a first-generation Korean abstract artist, contributing to the development of new expression styles in post-war Korea and establishing an art historical legacy. He graduated from the Tokyo Metropolitan Art School (now Musashino Art University) in Tokyo, Japan, and his fellow students at the time included Kim Jong-ha, Jang Wook-jin, and Byun Young-won. Kim Chang-eok later became an artist and educator in Seoul, teaching students at Gyeonggi Girls' High School (1954-1963) and Hongik University (1966-1987). Kim Chang-Eok's world of work is deeply influenced by Neo-Impressionism, Cubism, and the works of Wassily Kandinsky, and is a combination of Western art traditions and Korean culture. His work developed from symbolic abstraction in the 1950s and 1960s to figurative depictions of nature in the 1970s, and his reverence for the landscape and cultural heritage of Gyeongju, Gyeongsangbuk-do is particularly notable. He was also a founding member of Shinsanghoe, led by Yoo Young-guk, Lee Dae-won, and Lee Bong-sang, in 1962, and was awarded the Magnolia Medal of the National Merit in 1981. His work was recently reexamined by being included in a monumental exhibition (2023) held at the Gwacheon branch of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art.

Like other artists of his generation, Kim Chang-Eok has continued his artistic activities through various creative stages in line with the development of modern post-war Korea. Landscape painting was a constant source of inspiration throughout Kim Chang-Eok's artistic journey throughout his life, from the geometric and symbolic abstraction he devoted himself to for the first 30 years to the straightforward conception that stood out in his later years. The period from the late 1970s to the 1980s was a turning period that brought about this change in style, and it was during this period that the expression of the natural environment unfolded most dynamically. The understated subjectivity of the work combines picturesque mountains, forests, and streams with eye-catching immediacy and timeless charm.

Chang-Eok Kim's paintings, which shifted attention from images that had little to do with objective reality to more clearly recognizable landscapes, moved closer to the realm of simulacra while maintaining a certain degree of phenomenological affect. Rather than insisting on a single, authoritative perspective, Chang-Eok Kim cleverly synthesized the different but co-existing perceptual paradigms of reality and representation to derive a perspective that they simultaneously share. As a result, Kim Chang-Eok's abstracted landscapes evoke similar sensory responses despite not attempting to replicate "real" landscapes.

About Lehmannmuffin:
Founded in New York by Rachel Lehmann and David Maupin in 1996, Lehmann Maupin has continued to serve as a leading contemporary art gallery since its opening and has sought geographic expansion into the United States, Europe, and Asia. Over the past 30 years, Lehmann Maupin has played a pivotal role in introducing international artists to new territories and building lasting curatorial relationships. Known for championing diverse artistic voices, the gallery's program proudly showcases artists who challenge discourses surrounding identity and create new global cultures. Currently, the gallery has permanent exhibition spaces in New York, Seoul, and London, and teams in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore, and Palm Beach. Recently, Lehman Muffin opened seasonal exhibition spaces in Aspen, Palm Beach, Taipei, Beijing, and Milan to keep pace with growth opportunities in new markets.

(Info from Lehmann Maupin – New York, Seoul, London)

reviews.author: un promeneur solitaire
reviews.text:
MIRYU YOON: Do Wetlands Scare You?
2024. 08. 23 ~ 2024. 10. 05

Foundry Seoul is pleased to present Do Wetlands Scare You?, a solo exhibition by Seoul-based artist Yoon Mi-ryu, from August 23 to October 5, 2024. presents. Mi-Ryu Yoon, who explores in pictorial language the unique impressions and abstract senses that appear momentarily as a character interacts with the space surrounding him, introduces 33 new works set in a swamp in this exhibition.

‘A place where the ground is hollow and there is always water.’ Swamps are a habitat for various animals and plants and are a symbol of vitality that is essential to nature. However, at the same time, the swamp, which is a tangle of clay and submerged plants, is an object of fear and fear for humans because once one falls into it, an adult can be submerged in an instant and it is difficult to escape. In this exhibition, Mi-Ryu Yoon continues his pictorial experiments using the swamp as a symbolic space.

Yun Mi-ryu's paintings contain people and situations and can be classified into figurative paintings and portrait paintings. However, in reality, the artist's goal is not to depict the subject in detail like a traditional portrait, but to capture the unique formativeness and abstract sense created by a person's interaction with the environment and experiment with this using pictorial language. Therefore, the characters in Yun Mi-ryu's works do not exist as subjects leading a continuous narrative. They are a medium that reveals the senses the artist wants to capture and explore, and they are an intermediary that presents the beginnings of a new narrative that will expand infinitely in the viewer's imagination.

For this work, Mi-Ryu Yoon carries out a unique process. The author recruits close acquaintances, such as colleagues, friends, and younger siblings, as characters in the work and makes them move in carefully staged situations. At this time, backgrounds, objects, clothing, and tools are selected with careful consideration of color and material properties in order to maximize the senses desired to be revealed. Afterwards, the artist converts the staged scene into an image using the iPhone's Live Photo function. A live photo records the situation 1.5 seconds before and after the moment it was taken. In this process, the image, which is a mixture of familiar objects and unfamiliar sensations, combines thoroughly staged scenes with accidental elements such as light, temperature, and momentary expressions and movements. The artist translates the abstract sensations captured in such a moment and converted into images into pictorial language. As a result, Yun Mi-ryu's canvas becomes an illusion as a collection of senses, and the characters on the canvas interact with other subjects surrounding them, creating new senses and becoming a medium that draws the audience into an expanded experience.

In this exhibition, Mi-Ryu Yoon focuses on women living in swamps who have seductive or destructive powers. The swamp, with its eerie and gloomy atmosphere created by dense jungle and a wetland with an unknown bottom, has been the setting for various tales and myths. And there, spirits, fairies, monsters, and ghosts that threaten humans often appear. Although their forms and characteristics vary depending on the region or culture, they are mostly depicted as unique spiritual beings who remain near the water and drag humans into the water and drive them to death.

In Slavic mythology, Rusalka, who appears either as an old woman covered in fur or as a woman with sparkling eyes, long green hair, and a slippery body, seduces men and dances with them until they die at the water's edge, or drags them into the water and tickles them to drown. Näkki, a beautiful figure in Finnish mythology with long, flowing hair, can transform her appearance at will, and when the sun sets, she transforms into a monster with scales, protruding eyes, and sharp teeth, and drags children into the water to drown them. They evolved through various stories and instilled anxiety and fear in people, while also becoming symbolic beings that protected people from danger.

Rather than viewing these beings as evil spirits or ruthless and violent witches who harm humans without reason, Mi-Ryu Yoon explores their multi-layered context and is interested in the power and mystery they possess. And the author seeks to reveal a new aspect of the myth with three women against the backdrop of a swamp. One woman calls out to another in the water. They stare at the audience or at each other, whisper messages, hold hands, and hug each other. In a huge canvas that overwhelms the audience, their movements create rippling waves and pull the viewer into the illusion. But the ending of this story is not death. The women in the eye-catching canvas are no longer Rusalka or Nacky. They exist with us now, creating new sensations using their whole bodies at every moment. In Yun Mi-ryu's screen, layer by layer, layered with heavy brush strokes, they constantly ignite the spark of life by presenting attractive clues toward a new narrative that the audience can imagine.

‘Today’s Joy’_Himuro Yuri Exhibition

It was interesting to see the works that expressed various things such as the sea, mountains, objects, and people using fabric and thread. It was an exhibition that highlighted the artist's imagination and effort. The pattern of the fabric and the texture and lines of the thread felt different from oil paintings.

reviews.author: Son Joo-il (Cecil)
reviews.text:
Himuro Yuri’s Joy of the Day exhibition held at Ground Seesaw Hannam was truly a time that literally brightened my heart.
From the moment I opened the door to the exhibition hall and entered, I could feel the temperature of light and color permeating the entire space. A feeling of air pervaded the entire exhibition, as if the artist's warm fingertips had warmly embraced the coldness of the transparency unique to the material called glass.
The spatial composition was particularly excellent, with different emotions flowing naturally in each area, while the theme of the exhibition, ‘Today’s Joy’, flowed consistently. On one side, there was a space that seemed to recreate the artist's studio, and on the other side, the reflection scene created by light breaking on glass was so beautiful. Each little sparkle resembled the calm happiness of everyday life.
In the space where Himuro Yuri's introduction video was shown, I stopped walking for a moment. As I watched the artist describe the process of his work and the time it took for a piece of glass to become a work of art, I could feel the delicate warmth of the material called glass before it cools down and hardens. I don't think I'll ever forget the scene where glass melts in a fire and is reborn as light through the artist's fingertips.
When I watched the works again after the video was over, they were completely different from when I first saw them. I thought this is what it means to know and see. As I could feel the time and care put into each piece, I felt as if I was looking at small lives. Even the tiny bubbles hidden within the transparent object seemed like a language containing the artist's story.
And the production process video in the second half was really interesting. The sound of melting glass, the rhythm of tools clashing, and the artist's concentrated expression on screen were unfamiliar yet strangely comfortable. After watching the process, I felt like the works in the exhibition hall were not just objects, but records of time and temperature.
It was also great that the atmosphere of the exhibition continued until the last goods space. Small keyrings made of glass, mini objects, and warm handwritten phrases perfectly completed the exhibition's sensibility. It was not just a pretty souvenir, but it felt like I was holding in my hands the ‘joy of today’ that the exhibition was trying to convey.
Overall, I got the impression that this exhibition was created with a great balance between ‘cuteness’ and ‘refined sensibility’. It is a beauty that permeates calmly rather than stimulating emotions. I don't know if that's why I felt so relieved on the way out of the exhibition hall.
Ground Seesaw Hannam's sense of space and Himuro Yuri's delicate world could come together so well. It was an exhibition that I was satisfied with in every aspect for the first time in a long time.
A gentle smile stayed on my face the entire time I was watching it, and it was a day where I could fully feel the ‘joy of today’, as the exhibition title suggests.

Himuro Yuri
I was worried about whether to come or not because I was disappointed with the exhibition I saw at Ground Seesaw Central in the past, but it was a good decision to visit. This is the opening exhibition of Ground Seesaw Hannam.
I am a textile designer, and it was interesting to record my daily life using a unique technique (Snip Snap*). These works are made like writing a diary. The content of each section was good, but I liked the sea theme the best. (Dogs also surf...)
In the middle, I saw an inversion table and a hanbok, so I thought, 'What is it?' I wanted to. However, the author said that he turned what he remembered from his trip to Korea into a work of art. Towards the end of the exhibition, there are some works created for the Korean exhibition.
Some of the works are so large that they almost cover the wall, so it's fun to look at them one by one up close. There are two works that you can touch with your own hands. Don't pass by and touch it once in a while. The souvenir shop also has products you can make yourself. It's cute and adorable.
The artist's video was playing in one corner of the space. The same video is also uploaded to YouTube. So, it would be nice to see the exhibition one more time on the way home.
It's a bit complicated to find the entrance to the exhibition hall, but it's clean and spacious.

I don't have a juicer at home, so I couldn't make juice even if I wanted to, but I've been drinking it after getting it delivered from Organica. Chewy roasted sweet potatoes are also good as a meal replacement to help with diet. I also enjoy eating Honest Bar for breakfast. Now that I think about it, I always eat Organica products at least once a day. Thank you as always for a good product.

reviews.author: seaweed snack tv
reviews.text: This time, I did the Total Cleanse for 3 days and it had a good detoxifying effect and I was really satisfied. Do you call a counselor with questions while doing the cleanse? The people were very kind and explained step by step. They all seemed to be cleanse masters. I buy chewy roasted sweet potatoes and rice from the Organica website, and I use them very well because they are organic and can be healthy. I will recommend it to people around me~

reviews.author: Jeong Kyeong-mo
reviews.text:
I don't know if sales have skyrocketed due to Hong Jeong-wook's personal image, but it is true that the sweet potatoes I sometimes buy at my local CVS taste good, but the neat angles and colors of the beginning have disappeared. I understand and fully support this company's pursuit of being eco-friendly and close to nature.
However, I think that sweet potatoes are expensive and rice is too expensive. I hope to break away from the impact on the national economy, price stability, and the bad precedent of Starbucks coming in and raising the price of coffee to the same level as the price of a meal, and become a company with 1 trillion won in sales through various creative methods such as a change in idea or overseas expansion.
If the price of rice eaten by all people rises, all prices will rise.
Something big is happening to the country's economy.

reviews.author: Dosa Almond
reviews.text:
Thanks to Sooyoung Choi, who handed out business ticket-type brochures, I was able to experience the new brand and new features.
Since it was on sale, I felt like it was good value for money.
I can clearly see that travelers no longer need to buy a neck pillow.
It might become a must-have item for officers.
It was a functional clothing item that was great to buy as a gift for friends when returning home.
